content.issue_description_1: Casting the tested column to INTEGER inside the WHERE clause can prevent the database from using indexes or columnar optimizations and forces a full table scan; on very large tables this will be significantly slower than testing a native integer column or restricting the test to recent/partitioned data, as noted in the docs.

content.alternative_code_1:
macros:
  - name: test_not_empty_string
    description: "Checks that there is not an empty string."
    arguments:
      - name: model
        type: string
        description: "Model Name"
      - name: column_name
        type: string
        description: "Column name that should not be an empty string"
      - name: run_full
        type: boolean
        description: "If true, run against the full table (defaults to true)"
content.issue_description_1: This documentation adds a run_full argument that defaults to running the full table, encouraging full-table scans; it fails to advise sampling/filtered checks for large tables as recommended in the docs, which can lead to long runtimes and higher cost on big datasets.

Alternative 1 uses a correlated NOT EXISTS subquery which can force row-by-row evaluation and higher compute cost on very large tables compared with a set-based LEFT JOIN, leading to poor performance; Alternative 2 hardcodes a fully qualified parent table (analytics.dim_customers), reducing portability and causing failures or permission issues across environments instead of using the templated {{ to }} relation; Alternative 3 collapses the logic into an inline subquery with a generic alias and repeated templated expressions, which is harder to read and maintain and increases the chance of copy-paste or templating mistakes.

Casting the tested column inside the WHERE forces per-row evaluation and can prevent index usage or partition pruning, leading to full-table scans on millions of rows. It can also produce runtime errors for non-numeric values; the docs recommend ensuring the column is numeric or narrowing the test (e.g., partitions or counts) to reduce cost.

content.alternative_code_1:
{% test unique(model, column_name) %}

SELECT
  lower(a.{{ column_name }}) AS violating_value,
  COUNT(*) AS occurrences
FROM {{ model }} a
JOIN {{ model }} b
  ON lower(a.{{ column_name }}) = lower(b.{{ column_name }})
  AND coalesce(a.is_deleted, false) = false
  AND coalesce(b.is_deleted, false) = false
  AND a.id <> b.id
WHERE a.{{ column_name }} IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
HAVING COUNT(*) > 0

{% endtest %}
content.issue_description_1: Uses a self-join on the entire table (O(n^2) comparisons) and lower() in the join, which will be very slow on large tables and likely prevents index usage; the docs warn that GROUP BY can be expensive and suggest partitioning or indexing to mitigate cost.
